subject: OS
prompt: Aisha's laptop has 4 cores and about 200 programs loaded. What is the OS mainly doing about this?

options.label: Running all 200 programs at the same time on 4 cores
Rapidly switching the cores between programs so all of them make progress
Refusing to start programs 5 onwards until a core is free
Splitting each core into 50 smaller cores

explanation: With 4 cores, the OS switches them rapidly between programs so each makes progress; nothing truly runs 200 at once.

subject: OS
prompt: Which of these is the "illusionist" job of an OS?

options.label: Stopping the compiler from overwriting the browser's memory
Turning "save file" into disk block writes
Making each app behave as if it owns the whole laptop
Loading the kernel into RAM at boot

explanation: The illusionist job is giving every app the false impression that it owns the whole machine.

subject: OS
prompt: Why can the kernel not simply start itself when the laptop powers on?

options.label: The kernel is encrypted until the user logs in
The kernel is a file on the SSD, and RAM is empty at power-on
The kernel only runs in user mode
The CPU cannot execute kernel code until a driver is installed

explanation: RAM is volatile and empty at power-on, so the kernel file has to be copied in from the SSD by something else first.

subject: OS
prompt: Aisha closes her lid and reopens it two minutes later; her desktop appears in one second. Why is this faster than the 18-second boot?

options.label: The bootloader caches the kernel on the SSD
The firmware skips its hardware checks after the first boot
RAM stayed powered, so the kernel and her apps were never unloaded
The login program was disabled

explanation: Sleep keeps RAM powered, so the kernel and apps are still loaded and nothing has to be fetched from disk again.

subject: OS
prompt: The editor executes an instruction that talks straight to the SSD controller. What happens?

options.label: The instruction runs, but slowly
The CPU refuses it because the editor is in user mode, and the OS steps in
The OS silently rewrites it into a system call
The instruction runs only if the file is smaller than 4 KB

explanation: Talking to a device is a privileged instruction; in user mode the CPU refuses it and hands control to the OS.

subject: OS
prompt: Which pair correctly describes a system call?

options.label: Same mode, different program
Different mode, same program
Different — mode, different program
Same mode, same program

explanation: A system call flips the CPU from user to kernel mode while the same program keeps the CPU.

subject: OS
prompt: The compile job runs an infinite loop and makes no system calls. What stops it from freezing the laptop?

options.label: The OS polls every program once a second
The timer interrupt forces the CPU into the kernel periodically
The compiler is required to yield voluntarily
The kernel runs on a reserved fifth core

explanation: The hardware timer fires every few milliseconds and forces entry into the kernel regardless of what the program is doing.

subject: OS
prompt: A program divides by zero. What is this called?

options.label: An interrupt, because the CPU stops
A trap, because the kernel is entered
An exception, because the running instruction caused it
A system call, because control moves to the kernel

explanation: An exception is caused by the instruction currently executing, unlike an interrupt which comes from unrelated hardware.

subject: OS
prompt: Aisha runs gcc in two terminals at once. How many heaps exist?

options.label: One, shared between both
Two, one per process
One per CPU core
None until the program calls for memory

explanation: Each launch creates a separate process with its own complete address space, so there are two heaps.

subject: OS
prompt: Which section of a process's address space holds the trail of function calls?

options.label: Code
Data
Heap
Stack

explanation: The stack holds local variables and pushes a frame for every function call.

subject: OS
prompt: The browser's network reply finally arrives. What state does it move to?

options.label: Running, immediately
Ready, and it queues for a core
New, because it restarts its request
Terminated, because the request is done

explanation: There is only one arrow into Running and it starts at Ready, so the browser must queue for a core.

subject: OS
prompt: The compile job's 4 ms time slice expires. Which transition happens?

options.label: Running to Waiting
Running to Terminated
Running to Ready
Ready to Waiting

explanation: The timer interrupt takes the core back, but the process is still perfectly able to run.

subject: OS
prompt: The editor makes a read system call that returns immediately from cache. What happened?

options.label: A context switch, because the kernel ran
A mode switch only, because the same process kept the CPU
Both, because every system call switches processes
Neither, because cached reads skip the kernel

explanation: The same process kept the CPU and only the privilege level changed.

subject: OS
prompt: Why is a very short time slice a bad idea?

options.label: Processes would never finish their work
The PCB would grow too large to store
The 5 us switching cost would become a large share of the total time
The ready queue would run out of space

explanation: The 5 us switch is fixed overhead, so the shorter the slice, the larger a fraction of time is wasted.

subject: OS
prompt: Why is switching between two threads of the same process cheaper than switching between two processes?

options.label: Threads have smaller PCBs to copy
The memory map does not have to change
Threads never use CPU registers
The kernel is not involved in either case

explanation: Threads share one address space, so the expensive memory map switch is skipped.

subject: OS
prompt: The browser is blocked waiting for a network reply. Is the scheduler considering it?

options.label: Yes, it is in the ready queue
No, it is Waiting, so a core would be useless to it
Yes, but only if no CPU-bound process is available
No, because it has already terminated

explanation: Only Ready processes are scheduling candidates; a Waiting process needs an event, not a core.

subject: OS
prompt: Which piece of hardware makes preemptive scheduling possible?

options.label: The disk controller
The memory management unit
The timer interrupt
The second CPU core

explanation: Without a timer interrupt the OS could never take a core back from a program that makes no system calls.

subject: OS
prompt: A process arrives at 3 ms, first gets the core at 10 ms, and finishes at 11 ms. What is its waiting time?

options.label: 1 ms
7 ms
8 ms
11 ms

explanation: Turnaround is 11 - 3 = 8, and waiting is turnaround minus the 1 ms burst.

subject: OS
prompt: Why can a real OS not simply use SJF?

options.label: SJF produces worse average waiting times than FCFS
SJF needs the burst length in advance, which the OS does not know
SJF requires a preemptive timer, which not all CPUs have
SJF cannot handle processes that arrive at different times

explanation: SJF assumes future knowledge the OS does not have, so real systems can only estimate it.

subject: OS
prompt: Under Round Robin with a 4 ms quantum, the compile job is cut off after 4 ms with 4 ms remaining. Where does it go?

options.label: To the front of the ready queue
To the back of the ready queue
To the waiting queue until I/O completes
It keeps the core, since it has not finished

explanation: The queue rotates; sending a preempted process to the front would let it monopolise the core.

subject: OS
prompt: The Nova-14's quantum is lowered from 4 ms to 50 us. What happens?

options.label: Turnaround improves because jobs finish sooner
Nothing changes, since the same jobs still run
Roughly 9% of CPU time is lost to context switching
Round Robin becomes non-preemptive

explanation: With a 5 us switch against a 50 us quantum, about 5 of every 55 us is overhead.

subject: OS
prompt: With a quantum of 8 ms, our four jobs produce exactly the FCFS schedule. Why?

options.label: 8 ms is the length of the longest burst, so nobody is ever cut off
Round Robin ignores the quantum when jobs arrive at different times
The scheduler switches to FCFS when the queue is short
Context switches become free at large quanta

explanation: Every burst fits inside one quantum, so no process is ever preempted and the rotation never happens.

subject: OS
prompt: Under MLFQ, the code editor's 1 ms burst finishes well inside its 1 ms top-queue turn... and then it blocks waiting for the next keypress. What happens to it?

options.label: It is demoted, because it used the core
It stays in the top queue, because it blocked before its quantum ended
It is promoted above the top queue
It is removed from the queues until Aisha types

explanation: Blocking early is the signal that a process is interactive, so MLFQ keeps it at a high priority.

subject: OS
prompt: A process is waiting for a resource that another process will never release. Is this starvation?

options.label: Yes, and aging would fix it
Yes, but only if priorities are involved
No, it is deadlock, and aging would not help
No, it is preemption

explanation: It is waiting on a resource rather than on a turn, so raising its priority changes nothing.

subject: OS
prompt: What does aging change about a waiting process?

options.label: Its burst time
Its priority
Its arrival time
Its quantum

explanation: Aging raises priority with waiting time, which is what guarantees nothing waits forever.

subject: OS
prompt: Why can bytes_loaded = bytes_loaded + 1 be interrupted halfway?

options.label: Because the variable is stored on the heap
Because it compiles to three machine instructions, not one
Because the two threads run on different cores
Because addition is a slow operation

explanation: Read, add and write are separate instructions, and preemption can land between any two of them.

subject: OS
prompt: Three threads only ever read a shared value; none writes to it. Is this a race condition?

options.label: Yes, any shared access is a race
Yes, if they run on different cores
No, a race needs at least one writer
No, but only if the value is small enough

explanation: Concurrent reads of an unchanging value are always safe; a race needs a writer.

subject: OS
prompt: A locking scheme guarantees only one thread is ever inside, but one unlucky thread is repeatedly overtaken and never gets in. Which requirement is violated?

options.label: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting
None; it is correct

explanation: Bounded waiting is the requirement that limits how often others can enter ahead of you.

subject: OS
prompt: Why should a critical section be kept as short as possible?

options.label: Long ones use more memory
Every other thread is blocked for its whole duration
The compiler cannot optimise long sections
The scheduler refuses sections longer than one quantum

explanation: Every instruction inside the fence is time during which all other threads are stuck.

subject: OS
prompt: Two threads call test_and_set on a free lock at the same instant. What do they get back?

options.label: Both get 0
Both get 1
One gets 0 and the other gets 1
The result is undefined

explanation: Test-and-set is atomic, so the two calls are serialised and only one can see the free lock.

subject: OS
prompt: A thread expects to wait about 300 ns for a lock. Context switching costs 5 us. Which is better?

options.label: A blocking mutex, because sleeping is always cheaper
A spinlock, because the wait is far shorter than a switch
Neither; 300 ns is too short to need a lock
A blocking mutex, because spinlocks are unsafe

explanation: Sleeping and waking would cost far more than the 300 ns wait itself.

subject: OS
prompt: A semaphore starts at 3. Four threads call wait in quick succession. What happens to the fourth?

options.label: It gets a permit, since the count wraps around
It sleeps until another thread calls signal
It receives an error and continues
It spins until the count becomes negative

explanation: The count is 0, so the fourth thread blocks until a permit is returned.

subject: OS
prompt: What value would you initialise a semaphore to if you want it to act as a lock?

options.label: The number of threads

explanation: Starting at 1 means exactly one thread can hold it at a time.

subject: OS
prompt: In the producer, why must wait(empty) come before wait(mutex)?

options.label: Because empty is a counting semaphore and must always go first
Otherwise a full buffer makes the producer sleep while holding the mutex
Because the consumer checks mutex first
To keep empty and full adding up to 4

explanation: Sleeping while holding the mutex leaves the consumer unable to make room, which deadlocks both.

subject: OS
prompt: The buffer has 4 slots and 2 are filled. What are the semaphore values?

options.label: empty = 4, full = 4, mutex = 1
empty = 2, full = 2, mutex = 1
empty = 0, full = 2, mutex = 0
empty = 2, full = 4, mutex = 2

explanation: The counts are literally the free slots and the filled slots, and the mutex is unheld.

subject: OS
prompt: A deadlocked pair of processes is running on the Nova-14. What does CPU usage look like?

options.label: Pinned at 100%, since both are looping
Near zero, since both are in the Waiting state
Exactly 50%, one core each
It rises steadily until the OS intervenes

explanation: Deadlocked processes sit in Waiting and consume no CPU, which is what makes deadlock easy to miss.

subject: OS
prompt: Which condition is broken if a resource can be forcibly taken back from the process holding it?

options.label: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait

explanation: No preemption means the resource can only be released voluntarily, so forcible reclaim breaks it.

subject: OS
prompt: A resource allocation graph shows no cycle. What can you conclude?

options.label: Nothing, without knowing instance counts
There is definitely no deadlock
There is definitely a deadlock
There may be a deadlock among multi-instance resources

explanation: The absence of a cycle rules out deadlock regardless of how many instances each resource has.

subject: OS
prompt: An arrow points from a process to a resource. What does it mean?

options.label: The process is holding that resource
The process is requesting that resource and is waiting
The resource has been preempted from the process
The process has released the resource

explanation: An arrow out of a process is a request, which means the process is waiting for that resource.

subject: OS
prompt: Available is 3, 3, 4. Which process can be run first in a safe sequence, given the Need values 7 4 3 (music), 1 2 2 (browser), 6 0 0 (editor), 0 1 1 (compile)?

options.label: The music player, since it needs the most
Either the browser or the compile job
The editor, since it needs no file handles
None of them; the state is unsafe

explanation: Both 1 2 2 and 0 1 1 fit inside the available 3 3 4, so either can safely go first.

subject: OS
prompt: The Banker's algorithm denies a request even though the resources are free. Why?

options.label: The requesting process has exceeded its declared maximum
Granting it would leave a state with no safe sequence
The resources are reserved for higher-priority processes
The process is already deadlocked

explanation: Avoidance refuses any state from which every process could no longer be guaranteed to finish.

subject: OS
prompt: Which prevention technique is actually used in real concurrent programs?

options.label: Requiring all resources to be requested up front
Making every resource shareable
Numbering locks and always acquiring them in increasing order
Forcibly preempting open files

explanation: Lock ordering breaks circular wait, costs nothing at runtime, and only requires an agreed convention.

subject: OS
prompt: A system is in an unsafe state. What follows?

options.label: A deadlock has already occurred
A deadlock will definitely occur
A deadlock may occur, but might not
The state is impossible under the Banker's algorithm

explanation: Unsafe means deadlock is reachable, not that it has happened or must happen.

subject: OS
prompt: The compile job and the browser both access address 5000. What happens?

options.label: They read the same byte, which is a race condition
The MMU translates each to a different physical address
The second access fails with a protection error
The OS pauses one of them until the other finishes

explanation: Each process has its own translation table, so identical logical addresses land in different frames.

subject: OS
prompt: Why is address translation done in hardware rather than by the OS?

options.label: The OS does not know the physical addresses
Hardware translation is more secure
Running OS code on every memory access would be far too slow
The MMU can only be programmed by hardware

explanation: Address translation happens on every access, so any software involvement would dominate the cost.

subject: OS
prompt: Holes of 100, 500, 200, 300, 600 MB and a 212 MB request. Which hole does best fit choose?

options.label: 500 MB
300 MB
600 MB
200 MB

explanation: Best fit takes the smallest hole that is still large enough, which is 300 MB.

subject: OS
prompt: There is 1,700 MB free but a 700 MB request fails. What is this called?

options.label: Internal fragmentation
External fragmentation
Thrashing
A memory leak

explanation: The free memory exists but is split into pieces too small for the request.

subject: OS
prompt: With 4 KB pages, logical address 9,000 falls in which page, at what offset?

options.label: Page 2, offset 808
Page 3, offset 904
Page 2, offset 9000
Page 1, offset 4904

explanation: 9000 divided by 4096 gives page 2, and the remainder 808 is the offset.

subject: OS
prompt: Logical address 0x2328 translates to physical 0x7328. Why are the last three hex digits identical?

options.label: Coincidence caused by this particular page table
They are the offset, which is copied without translation
The MMU only translates even-numbered pages
Because frame 7 happens to start at address 0x7000

explanation: Only the page number is replaced by a frame number; the offset passes through untouched.

subject: OS
prompt: What does paging introduce that contiguous allocation did not have?

options.label: External fragmentation
Internal fragmentation and an extra memory access per reference
The need for compaction
A shared address space between processes

explanation: Fixed pieces waste part of the last page, and the page table must be read before the data.

subject: OS
prompt: TLB access is 10 ns, RAM is 100 ns, and the hit rate is 90%. What is the effective access time?

options.label: 110 ns
120 ns
200 ns
210 ns

subject: OS
prompt: Why is the TLB flushed on a context switch?

options.label: Its entries belong to the outgoing process and would be wrong
To free memory for the incoming process
Because the page size may change between processes
It is not flushed; it is shared between all processes

explanation: Translations are per process, so stale entries would map the new process to the wrong frames.

subject: OS
prompt: What does segmentation have that paging does not?

options.label: Freedom from external fragmentation
Pieces that correspond to meaningful parts of the program
A smaller lookup table
Hardware support in the MMU

explanation: Segments follow the program's own structure, which is what makes segment-level protection meaningful.

subject: OS
prompt: What does the valid bit in a page table entry indicate?

options.label: Whether the process is allowed to write to the page
Whether the page is currently in RAM
Whether the page has been modified since loading
Whether the page belongs to the running process

explanation: The valid bit says whether the page is resident; if not, the frame number is meaningless.

subject: OS
prompt: Why can a program be larger than the Nova-14's physical RAM?

options.label: The OS compresses pages before loading them
Only the pages currently being used need to be resident
The MMU allocates extra frames on demand
Unused pages are deleted from the program

explanation: Demand paging keeps only the touched pages resident, so the address space can exceed physical RAM.

subject: OS
prompt: Memory access is 100 ns and a page fault costs 100,000 ns. With a fault rate of 0.001, what is the effective access time?

subject: OS
prompt: Why is the faulting instruction restarted rather than resumed?

options.label: The CPU forgets the instruction during the trap
It never completed, so there is no partial state to continue from
Restarting is faster than saving the partial result
The page may have loaded into a different frame

explanation: The instruction was stopped before completing anything, so there is no partial state to resume from.

subject: OS
prompt: FIFO on the string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4. What is this called?

options.label: Thrashing
Belady's anomaly
The convoy effect
External fragmentation

explanation: Belady's anomaly is more frames producing more faults, which only non-stack algorithms like FIFO can show.

subject: OS
prompt: Why can the Optimal algorithm not be used in a real OS?

options.label: It is too slow to compute
It requires knowing which pages will be referenced in future
It suffers from Belady's anomaly
It needs hardware support that does not exist

explanation: Choosing the page needed furthest ahead requires the future reference string.

subject: OS
prompt: Why do real systems approximate LRU instead of implementing it exactly?

options.label: Exact LRU produces more faults than the approximation
Exact LRU would need bookkeeping on every memory access
Exact LRU exhibits Belady's anomaly
The page table has no room for timestamps

explanation: Exact LRU means updating ordering information on every single memory reference.

subject: OS
prompt: During thrashing, what does CPU utilisation look like?

options.label: Very high, since the OS is working hard
Very low, since most processes are blocked on the disk
Exactly 100%, split between swapping and executing
Unchanged from normal operation

explanation: Nearly every process is in Waiting on a page fetch, so almost nothing is ready to run.

subject: OS
prompt: The last six references were 3, 2, 5, 5, 6, 5. What is the working set for a window of 6?
explanation: The working set is the distinct pages in the window, so repeats collapse to one entry each.

subject: OS
prompt: A machine is thrashing. Which action would make it worse?

options.label: Adding more physical RAM
Suspending some processes
Increasing the swap space so more processes can be loaded
Reducing the number of running programs

explanation: More swap lets the OS admit more processes, which increases memory pressure and deepens the spiral.

subject: OS
prompt: Aisha renames a 12 KB file. Why is it instant?

options.label: The OS defers the copy until the file is next read
Only a directory entry changes; the inode and data are untouched
12 KB is small enough to copy in under a millisecond
The file is cached in RAM at the time

explanation: The name lives in the directory table, so renaming never touches the inode or the data blocks.

subject: OS
prompt: The editor and the compile job both have build.log open. What do they share?

options.label: The file descriptor number
The current offset
The inode, but not the offset
Nothing; each gets a private copy

explanation: There is one inode per file, but each open gets its own entry holding its own offset.

subject: OS
prompt: Why is random access slow with linked allocation?

options.label: The blocks are stored in reverse order
Each block's location is only known from the previous block
The index block must be read before every access
Linked blocks cannot be cached

explanation: Every block is found only through its predecessor, so reaching block n means reading n blocks.

subject: OS
prompt: With 12 direct pointers and 4 KB blocks, what is the largest file that needs no indirect block?

options.label: 4 KB
48 KB
4 MB
1,024 blocks

explanation: 12 direct pointers at 4 KB per block covers 48 KB before an indirect block is needed.

subject: OS
prompt: Head at 53, queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. What is the total head movement under FCFS?
explanation: Serving 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 in arrival order from 53 totals 640 tracks.

subject: OS
prompt: What is the main weakness of SSTF?

options.label: It always moves the head further than FCFS
A distant request can be starved indefinitely
It only works on solid state drives
It requires knowing future requests

explanation: SSTF always favours nearby requests, so a distant one can be passed over indefinitely.

subject: OS
prompt: Why does disk scheduling matter far less on an SSD?

options.label: SSDs serve requests in parallel
There is no head to move, so block position barely affects access time
SSDs reorder requests internally using SCAN
SSDs have much larger blocks

explanation: With no mechanical head, seek time disappears and the order of blocks stops mattering.

subject: OS
prompt: With DMA, how many interrupts does a 350-block transfer generate?

options.label: 350, one per block
One, at the end of the whole transfer
None; DMA does not use interrupts
Two, one at the start and one at the end

explanation: The DMA controller transfers everything itself and interrupts once when the whole job is done.

subject: OS
prompt: Which best describes the page cache?

options.label: A buffer that smooths the size mismatch between disk blocks and reads
A cache holding copies of recently used disk blocks in spare RAM
A region of swap space reserved for evicted pages
The DMA controller's staging area

explanation: It keeps copies of blocks already read, so a repeat read is served from RAM.

subject: OS
prompt: A program writes to build.log and the call returns immediately. Where is the data?

options.label: On the SSD, since writes are synchronous
In the page cache in RAM, not yet on the SSD
In the DMA controller's registers
In the process's own stack

explanation: Writes are absorbed by the page cache and flushed later, which is why they feel instant.

subject: OS
prompt: In the trace, what moved the editor from Waiting to Ready?

options.label: The scheduler's timer interrupt
The keyboard interrupt handler
The fork() system call
A page fault on the editor's code

explanation: The keyboard's interrupt handler stored the key and marked the editor Ready.

subject: OS
prompt: The compile job ran for 3.2 seconds. What was the CPU doing during its page faults?

options.label: Idling until the SSD replied
Running another process, since the compile job was in Waiting
Copying the page byte by byte
Flushing the TLB repeatedly

explanation: A faulting process is in Waiting, so the scheduler hands the core to somebody else.

subject: OS
prompt: Which module's work appears nowhere in the timeline as an event?

options.label: Module 3, because scheduling is invisible
Module 6, because address translation happens on every access
Module 8, because DMA needs no CPU
Module 5, because no deadlock occurred

explanation: Address translation happens on every access, so it underlies the whole trace rather than appearing as one event.

subject: OS
prompt: Which two beats of the answer frame should you protect if you are cut short?

options.label: Mechanism and trade-off
Define and example
Define and mechanism
Example and trade-off

explanation: The definition anchors the answer and the concrete example proves you have actually used the idea.

subject: OS
prompt: An interviewer asks about the TLB and you describe the speed benefit. What should you add unprompted?

options.label: The exact size of a typical TLB
That it is flushed on every context switch
The history of associative memory
A comparison with the L1 data cache

explanation: Naming the cost answers the follow-up before it is asked.

subject: OS
prompt: What is the strongest answer to a question you genuinely do not know?

options.label: Guess confidently and move on
Say you do not know and stop
Say you do not know, then connect it to something adjacent you do know
Change the subject to something you prepared

explanation: Admitting the gap and reasoning toward it shows judgement; bluffing shows the opposite.

subject: OS
prompt: A process is waiting for a lock that another process will never release. Aging is applied.

options.label: It eventually runs, because its priority rises
Nothing, because it is deadlocked, not starved
It is killed by the OS after a timeout
The lock is preempted from the holder

explanation: Aging raises priority, which does nothing for a process waiting on a resource that will never be released.

subject: OS
prompt: A program makes a read system call that is served from the page cache. How many context switches occurred?

options.label: Zero; only a mode switch happened
One, into the kernel
Two, in and back out
One per block read

explanation: The same process kept the CPU; only the privilege level changed.

subject: OS
prompt: With 4 KB pages, logical address 0x5ABC has what offset?

options.label: 0xABC
0x5AB
0xBC

explanation: With 4 KB pages the offset is the bottom 12 bits, which is the last three hex digits.

subject: OS
prompt: Which of these can exhibit Belady's anomaly?

options.label: LRU
Optimal
FIFO
All page replacement algorithms

explanation: FIFO is not a stack algorithm, so more frames can produce more faults.

subject: OS
prompt: Two threads of the browser both read a shared counter and neither writes. Is this a race condition?

options.label: Yes, any concurrent access is a race
No, a race requires at least one writer
Only on a multi-core CPU
Only if the counter is on the heap

subject: OS
prompt: The Round Robin quantum is set to 8 ms and every process's burst is under 8 ms. What has Round Robin become?

options.label: SJF
SRTF
FCFS
Priority scheduling

subject: OS
prompt: A page table entry has its valid bit clear. What does the MMU do on access?

options.label: Returns zero
Raises a trap into the kernel
Allocates a new frame automatically
Reads the page directly from swap

subject: OS
prompt: SSTF is chosen for a disk with a continuous stream of nearby requests. What is the risk?

options.label: Head movement will exceed FCFS
A distant request is starved indefinitely
The disk will thrash
Requests will be served out of arrival order, which corrupts files

explanation: SSTF always favours the nearest request, so a far one can be passed over forever.

subject: OS
prompt: In the producer–consumer solution, the producer calls wait(mutex) before wait(empty).

options.label: The producer overwrites the oldest entry
The producer sleeps holding the mutex, and both threads deadlock
The consumer is signalled and makes room
wait(empty) fails and returns an error

subject: OS
prompt: Thrashing is occurring. Which single change makes it worse?

options.label: Adding physical RAM
Suspending a process
Adding swap space so more processes can be loaded
Reducing the degree of multiprogramming

explanation: More swap admits more processes, increasing memory pressure and deepening the spiral.

subject: OS
prompt: Which is true of a hard link?

options.label: It stores a path to the original file
It is a second directory entry pointing at the same inode
It breaks when the original is deleted

subject: OS
prompt: With DMA, what is the CPU doing during a 350-block transfer?

options.label: Copying each block into memory
Polling the controller for completion
Running other processes; it is uninvolved until the final interrupt
Handling one interrupt per block
